text.text: Aims: The November 2023 evacuation of Grindavík, Iceland, left families facing prolonged uncertainty about return.
We examined adolescent well-being before and after evacuation and changes in gaps with national peers between 2025 and 2026.
Methods: Repeated cross-sectional analyses used the 2023, 2025, and 2026 Icelandic Youth Study waves, adjusting for grade, gender, and non-Icelandic background.
The town's single school in 2023 provided the pre-evacuation benchmark, with models accounting for national time trends.
Adolescents who moved before evacuation provided a mobility benchmark.

Results: In 2025, evacuees reported lower life satisfaction and school belonging, more psychosomatic symptoms, and higher odds of school absence and past-30-day substance use than the national reference group.
The three well-being outcomes departed from the pre-evacuation pattern.
Life-satisfaction and belonging gaps were larger among girls than boys in 2025, but these gender differences narrowed by 2026.
Comparisons with prior movers suggested a distinct evacuation-related pattern in 2025 among evacuee girls, who reported lower life satisfaction and school belonging than prior-mover girls.

In 2026, psychosomatic symptoms (B = 0.29, 95% CI [0.08, 0.49]), absenteeism (OR = 1.81, 95% CI [1.26, 2.60]), and substance use (OR = 2.59, 95% CI [1.75, 3.84]) remained higher relative to the national reference group.
Life satisfaction and belonging were directionally lower, with intervals including zero.
Change estimates did not establish narrowing of the gaps.

The findings underscore the need for sustained educational and well-being support to address adolescents' social connections alongside their mental health during prolonged displacement, including in a Nordic welfare setting.
Natural disasters that unfold slowly can leave communities in prolonged uncertainty about whether, when, and how residents can or should return home.
The town of Grindavík on Iceland's Reykjanes Peninsula is such a case.
After several years of seismic unrest and nearby eruptions, Grindavík was evacuated on November 10 th 2023 as magma moved beneath the town causing major earthquakes (Parks et al., 2024).
text.formatted: After several years of seismic unrest and nearby eruptions, Grindavík was evacuated on November 10 th 2023 as magma moved beneath the town causing major earthquakes <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Parks et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: All 3,790 residents had to leave, and repeated eruptions over the following months made a return unlikely for most families (Alþingi, 2024).
text.formatted: All 3,790 residents had to leave, and repeated eruptions over the following months made a return unlikely for most families <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Alþingi, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: For more than two years, the civil protection authorities rated the town as high risk for families with children, before lowering the risk level in mid-year 2026 (Almannavarnir, 2026).
text.formatted: For more than two years, the civil protection authorities rated the town as high risk for families with children, before lowering the risk level in mid-year 2026 <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Almannavarnir, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In the immediate aftermath of the town's evacuation, authorities prioritised the immediate well-being and security of Grindavík residents.
Considerable emphasis was also on providing social and psychological support, not least for children and young people (Alþingi, 2024).
text.formatted: Considerable emphasis was also on providing social and psychological support, not least for children and young people <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Alþingi, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Schooling continued, at first partly in temporary Grindavík classes organized in the capital area and, from June 2024, in local schools across the country.

By fall 2024, Grindavík children were spread across 73 schools around Iceland, though the majority of Grindavík families had relocated either to the capital area or nearby municipalities on the Reykjanes peninsula (Framkvæmdanefnd Grindavíkur, 2025; for details, see Reimer et al., 2026).
text.formatted: By fall 2024, Grindavík children were spread across 73 schools around Iceland, though the majority of Grindavík families had relocated either to the capital area or nearby municipalities on the Reykjanes peninsula (Framkvæmdanefnd <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Grindavíkur, 2025</ref>; for details, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Reimer et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The town's school reopened in August 2026 with about 30 students, with most families remaining elsewhere (Víkurfréttir, 2026).
text.formatted: The town's school reopened in August 2026 with about 30 students, with most families remaining elsewhere <ref type="bibr">(Víkurfréttir, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: For adolescents, the evacuation meant losing a school community and neighbourhood friendships, moving home repeatedly, and settling into new schools, without knowing whether the move was temporary or permanent.
In the first five months after the evacuation, families changed homes about three times on average (Hrólfsson, 2024).
text.formatted: In the first five months after the evacuation, families changed homes about three times on average <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Hrólfsson, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: These disruptions occurred in a Nordic welfare setting which supported displaced families financially and provided access to education and social services.

The governmentappointed Grindavík Committee coordinated support for evacuated families and for the schools that received Grindavík students; its report described concern for emotional and social difficulties among students in host schools (Framkvæmdanefnd Grindavíkur, 2025).
text.formatted: The governmentappointed Grindavík Committee coordinated support for evacuated families and for the schools that received Grindavík students; its report described concern for emotional and social difficulties among students in host schools <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Framkvæmdanefnd Grindavíkur, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Among adults, a 2025 government survey found that 66% of evacuees reported worse mental health than before the evacuation and that 46% still regarded their housing as temporary (Forsætisráðuneytið, 2025).
text.formatted: Among adults, a 2025 government survey found that 66% of evacuees reported worse mental health than before the evacuation and that 46% still regarded their housing as temporary <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Forsætisráðuneytið, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Systematic evidence on the Grindavík adolescents comes so far from the 2025 wave of the Icelandic Youth Study, in which evacuees reported lower well-being than their peers nationally (Reimer et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Systematic evidence on the Grindavík adolescents comes so far from the 2025 wave of the Icelandic Youth Study, in which evacuees reported lower well-being than their peers nationally <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Reimer et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Like the reports above, it captures a single point in time and cannot show whether such differences are a transient reaction or the start of lasting difficulties.
The present study adds a pre-evacuation benchmark from the Grindavík school in 2023 and a second post-evacuation wave in 2026.
It asks which aspects of well-being recovered, which persisted, and for whom.

Disasters that disrupt the lives and schooling of school-aged children and adolescents are associated with poorer well-being and more psychosomatic complaints (Kousky, 2016; La Greca et al., 2023; Osofsky et al., 2009;  for a review see Auðardóttir & Gísladóttir, 2024).
text.formatted: Disasters that disrupt the lives and schooling of school-aged children and adolescents are associated with poorer well-being and more psychosomatic complaints <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Kousky, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">La Greca et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Osofsky et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr"/> for a review see <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Auðardóttir & Gísladóttir, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Similar consequences have followed other large disruptions of schooling, such as war and the COVID-19 pandemic (Bürgin et al., 2022; Betthäuser et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Similar consequences have followed other large disruptions of schooling, such as war and the COVID-19 pandemic <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Bürgin et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Betthäuser et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: These outcomes matter for adolescent health in their own right, and for students, well-being is also linked to learning (Bücker et al., 2018).
text.formatted: These outcomes matter for adolescent health in their own right, and for students, well-being is also linked to learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Bücker et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Displacement can disrupt several foundations of adolescents' well-being at once: friendships, belonging to a school community, family routines, and a sense of safety.
Recovery depends on how quickly these are rebuilt and on access to psychosocial services (Andrade et al., 2023; Abdi et al., 2023; Witt et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Recovery depends on how quickly these are rebuilt and on access to psychosocial services <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Andrade et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Abdi et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Witt et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Adolescents differ in their vulnerability and capacity to adapt, depending on individual, social, and contextual factors.
Schools, families, and peers can provide protective systems that help them cope with displacement (Abdi et al., 2023; Masten & Narayan, 2012).
text.formatted: Schools, families, and peers can provide protective systems that help them cope with displacement <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abdi et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Masten & Narayan, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Children's responses to disasters are also associated with parental stress and coping, further adversities after the disaster, and the social support available to them (Pfefferbaum et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Children's responses to disasters are also associated with parental stress and coping, further adversities after the disaster, and the social support available to them <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Pfefferbaum et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: This attention to disruption and adaptation informs our focus on life satisfaction, school belonging, psychosomatic complaints, substance use, and school absenteeism.
Post-disaster adjustment rarely follows a single trajectory.

Longitudinal research distinguishes stable resilience, gradual recovery, chronic difficulties, and delayed-onset problems rather than a uniform return to pre-disaster well-being (Bonanno et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Longitudinal research distinguishes stable resilience, gradual recovery, chronic difficulties, and delayed-onset problems rather than a uniform return to pre-disaster well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bonanno et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In a review of eight studies that followed children after natural disasters, all eight identified groups whose posttraumatic stress symptoms remained low, declined, or remained elevated.
Evidence for delayed onset was mixed (Lai et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Evidence for delayed onset was mixed <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Lai et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Two implications follow.
First, a gap observed at one point after evacuation may later shrink, persist, or widen.

Second, outcomes may not move together: global appraisals such as life satisfaction may rebound as new routines settle, while psychosomatic complaints or behavioural responses persist or emerge later.
Recovery may also differ according to families' socioeconomic status (see for example Lee and You, 2025) or between girls and boys.
text.formatted: Recovery may also differ according to families' socioeconomic status (see for example <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Lee and You, 2025)</ref> or between girls and boys.

text.text: Disaster studies often report stronger emotional reactions among girls (Pfefferbaum et al., 2015), and in the 2025 wave, the gaps in life satisfaction and school belonging among Grindavík evacuees were larger for girls than for boys (Reimer et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Disaster studies often report stronger emotional reactions among girls <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Pfefferbaum et al., 2015)</ref>, and in the 2025 wave, the gaps in life satisfaction and school belonging among Grindavík evacuees were larger for girls than for boys <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Reimer et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Less is known about whether such gender differences persist, narrow, or shift towards other outcomes as displacement continues.
While potentially relevant, an analysis of different patterns by socioeconomic status are outside the scope of the current study because the data only includes a subjective measure of family status.
This measure may be influenced not only by the displacement but also by how it influenced well-being.
Some of what follows an evacuation may reflect the student experience of moving as such rather than the disaster.
Migration and residential mobility in childhood have been linked to emotional and behavioural difficulties (Andrade et al., 2023; Cotton, 2016).
text.formatted: Migration and residential mobility in childhood have been linked to emotional and behavioural difficulties <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Andrade et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Cotton, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: One reason for this is that mobility disrupts students' friendship networks (South & Haynie, 2004), which are a major source of well-being among adolescents.
text.formatted: One reason for this is that mobility disrupts students' friendship networks <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(South & Haynie, 2004)</ref>, which are a major source of well-being among adolescents.

text.text: Students entering new schools also face a higher risk of peer victimization (Tenhunen et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Students entering new schools also face a higher risk of peer victimization <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Tenhunen et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Students who left Grindavík before the evacuation therefore offer a useful benchmark: difficulties shared with them may reflect mobility more generally, whereas difficulties found only among evacuees point more specifically to the evacuation.

At the same time, prior movers are a differently selected group relative to evacuees; in many cases differences between movers and non-movers may be explained by other disadvantages, including the neighbourhoods they live in and selection processes leading to mobility, such as family instability (Cotton, 2016).
text.formatted: At the same time, prior movers are a differently selected group relative to evacuees; in many cases differences between movers and non-movers may be explained by other disadvantages, including the neighbourhoods they live in and selection processes leading to mobility, such as family instability <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Cotton, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: In fact, previous research from Iceland on daily smoking among 15-16-year-olds found that adolescents who had moved to a new neighbourhood in the previous year were more likely to smoke daily than non-movers, even after adjusting for a range of family-and neighbourhood-level characteristics, including measures of social capital (Thorlindsson et al., 2012).
text.formatted: In fact, previous research from Iceland on daily smoking among 15-16-year-olds found that adolescents who had moved to a new neighbourhood in the previous year were more likely to smoke daily than non-movers, even after adjusting for a range of family-and neighbourhood-level characteristics, including measures of social capital <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Thorlindsson et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: This preregistered study uses the 2023, 2025, and 2026 waves of the Icelandic Youth Study to examine adolescent well-being after the Grindavík evacuation.
We compare evacuees with a national reference group and with students who left Grindavík before November 2023, referred to as prior movers.
The Grindavík school sample from 2023 provides a pre-evacuation benchmark.
We address three research questions: 1.
Do evacuees differ from the national reference group in life satisfaction, school belonging, psychosomatic symptoms, school absenteeism, and past-30-day substance use in 2025 and 2026?
Did these gaps change between waves, and do they differ by gender?

Do life satisfaction, school belonging, and psychosomatic symptoms among evacuees in 2025 and 2026 depart from levels observed in the Grindavík school in 2023, after accounting for national time trends?
Do comparisons with prior movers suggest a well-being pattern distinctive to evacuation, or difficulties shared with students who left Grindavík earlier?
The analyses estimate adjusted differences between surveyed groups at each wave and changes in those differences between 2025 and 2026.
Prior movers provide a mobility benchmark, and we use "evacuation-specific" to describe an observed pattern that distinguishes evacuees from prior movers.
These comparisons do not identify the causal effects or individual adjustment trajectories.
Continuing uncertainty about return provides context for interpreting the findings but is not directly measured.

We use repeated cross-sections from the Icelandic Youth Study (IYS), an annual nationwide school survey managed by the Educational Research Institute at the University of Iceland (Guðjohnsen et al., 2025).

School participation comprised 158 of 174 invited schools in 2023, 155 of 173 in 2025, and 153 schools in 2026.

In 2025 and 2026, three questions establish whether students had ever lived in Grindavík, whether they still did, and whether those who had left moved before or after November 2023.

Evacuees: students who lived in Grindavík and relocated in November 2023 or later, as well as those who still reported residing in Grindavík.

text.text: This study examined adolescent well-being after the Grindavík evacuation in two waves, both collected while the town was still rated high risk and return remained unresolved.
Before the evacuation, students at the Grindavík school reported well-being close to national levels.

In 2025, after national trends, evacuees' life satisfaction and school belonging were lower and their psychosomatic symptoms higher than this benchmark would suggest, and they reported more school absence and substance use than national peers.
In 2026, symptoms, absence, and substance use remained elevated, whereas the life-satisfaction and belonging gaps were smaller, with intervals including zero.
As the change estimates did not establish narrowing, this pattern indicates continuing difficulties rather than recovery.
The outcomes did not move together.
Between 2025 and 2026, the life-satisfaction and belonging gaps moved towards national levels, whereas the symptom gap remained of similar size relative to both national peers and the 2023 benchmark.

Although the change estimates did not establish narrowing, this pattern is consistent with asynchronous, domain-specific recovery, in which dimensions of well-being follow different trajectories after a disaster (Bonanno et al., 2024).

text.text: One reading of our findings is therefore that adolescents had largely re-established their social and school lives, whereas the strain of prolonged displacement and uncertainty remained present in body and mind.
Alternatively, symptoms may simply recover more slowly or reflect delayed responses; separating these explanations requires longitudinal data.
Either way, improvement in global well-being should not be read as a sign that the consequences of displacement have passed.
These gaps emerged under comparatively favourable conditions.
The Icelandic response combined financial support for displaced families, continued schooling, and psychosocial services within a well-resourced Nordic welfare state.
In many respects, the Grindavík evacuation thus approximates a best-case scenario for displaced adolescents.

That symptoms, school absence, and substance use nevertheless remained elevated more than two years later suggests that material security and institutional continuity, although necessary, do not by themselves protect adolescents from the strain of prolonged displacement.
Where support is weaker, the consequences are likely to be larger.

Evacuees and prior movers both reported more psychosomatic symptoms, school absence, and substance use than national peers in both years, and direct comparisons did not distinguish the two groups on these outcomes.

Although shared outcomes need not reflect shared processes, this similarity suggests that part of what follows an evacuation reflects relocation and school change more generally, consistent with research linking mobility to weaker school connectedness (Capp & Sullivan, 2020) and, in Iceland, to adolescent daily smoking (Thorlindsson et al., 2012).

text.text: Belonging is also where uncertainty about return might matter most.
Unlike most moves, the evacuation was involuntary and open-ended, so investing in a new school community may have seemed less worthwhile while ties to the former one persisted.
As uncertainty was not measured, this remains a hypothesis.

Practically, support should reach residentially mobile students whatever their reason for moving (Tenhunen et al., 2024), while evacuated students may additionally need help rebuilding a sense of belonging, a task in which schools are central (Smawfield, 2013).

text.text: Gender patterns differed across outcomes and changed over time.

In 2025, the lifesatisfaction and belonging gaps were larger for evacuee girls than boys, a pattern not visible at the 2023 benchmark, and evacuee girls were about half a standard deviation below prior-mover girls on both outcomes.
By 2026, these gender differences had narrowed, and girls' symptom gap was no longer evident, whereas boys' symptom and absence gaps persisted in both years.
Direct tests did not establish gender differences in absence or substance use.
Because the narrowing coincided with a fall in girls' share of the evacuee sample, it may partly reflect who participated rather than improved well-being.
The findings therefore argue against a general account of greater vulnerability among girls and for attention to outcomes and timing.
Because the data are repeated cross-sections, they cannot trace individual trajectories, and changes in group gaps may reflect changes in well-being, group composition, or participation.

Composition did shift between waves: girls' share of the evacuee sample fell from 42.3% to 36.7%, particularly in grades 9-10, while the 2026 prior movers included more girls and were younger on average.
Holding the 2025 evacuee gender-grade composition constant had little effect on the estimates, but neither this check nor covariate adjustment addresses selective participation within groups.
If girls with poorer well-being were less likely to participate in 2026, their gaps would be underestimated; whether this occurred is unknown.
The design is observational.

It cannot formally establish that the gaps were caused by the evacuation, separate the contributions of different housing and schooling arrangements, or identify disrupted school connections as the mechanism behind lower belonging.
Uncertainty about return, central to our interpretation, was not measured directly, and we do not know how students' expectations of return differed between individuals or changed between waves.
The pre-evacuation benchmark rests on a single school at one time point and cannot show whether Grindavík would otherwise have followed national trends.

Its 2023 sample includes students later classified as prior movers, and differences in analytic-sample standard deviations mean that benchmark and 2025-2026 coefficients are not directly comparable in magnitude.
The benchmark also does not cover school absence or substance use, so we cannot establish when those gaps emerged.
Questionnaire rotation restricted some analytic samples, and complete-case analysis may introduce selection if missing responses are related to well-being.
Harmonising symptom response categories does not establish measurement equivalence.
The home-language and IYSonly checks yielded smaller, less precise symptom estimates; because they also change sample composition, they cannot isolate response-scale effects.
Despite these limitations, the design makes several alternative explanations unlikely.
Because the whole town was evacuated, evacuees were not selected into displacement by family circumstances, as residential movers typically are.

The 2023 benchmark shows that Grindavík students did not stand out from their national peers before the evacuation, even after several years of seismic unrest, and the 2025 departures from that benchmark were estimated net of national time trends.
Pre-existing differences, national developments, or self-selection are therefore unlikely to account for the post-evacuation gaps.
Although the data cannot follow individuals over time, we consider the overall pattern difficult to reconcile with explanations unrelated to the displacement.
Natural disasters are a growing source of uncertainty in children's lives.

Climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of many weather-related hazards, and floods, storms, droughts, and wildfires already account for tens of millions of child displacements worldwide (IPCC, 2023; UNICEF, 2023).
Although the Grindavík crisis was geological, it shares a defining feature of many such displacements: an open-ended period of uncertainty about return.

This uncertainty concerns not only whether return will become safe, but also, as displacement lengthens and children settle into new schools and friendships, whether families will still want to go back.
As such events become more common, including in high-income countries, understanding how adolescents fare during this period becomes increasingly relevant for public health.

Our findings show that difficulties among displaced adolescents can outlast the immediate aftermath of an evacuation, even under close to best-case conditions of material support, schooling, and social services.
More than two years after leaving Grindavík, evacuees still reported more psychosomatic symptoms, school absence, and substance use than national peers.
These difficulties were shared with students who had moved for other reasons, whereas the main evacuation-specific contrast concerned school belonging.
Both waves captured a period in which return remained unresolved.

Since our data were collected, the formal barrier to return has been lifted: in summer 2026, Civil Protection lowered the town's risk level (Almannavarnir, 2026), and the Grindavík school reopened in August.

text.text: Yet only about 30 students enrolled, and most families remain elsewhere (Víkurfréttir, 2026).
After almost three years away, return is no longer the default.
The question has shifted from whether families can go back to whether they want to, and for many the answer appears to be no, or not yet.
For most adolescents, displacement is thus turning into permanent relocation, while for families who remain undecided, uncertainty continues in a new form.
Future waves can show whether gaps in belonging and well-being diminish as these situations settle.

Support for displaced adolescents should address not only material needs, symptoms, and continuity of schooling, but also friendships, attachment to school communities, and a sense of belonging as outcomes of recovery in their own right.
